title: Duck (nanásecus)
summary: Black ducks connect Long Island marshes with Shinnecock waterfowl knowledge and the art of decoy carving.
content:
Between marsh, water, and sky

The American black duck is a native waterbird of Long Island. Wertheim National Wildlife Refuge describes black ducks gathering on open water, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service identifies coastal salt marshes as important habitat. These ducks swim and fly between feeding and resting places.12

Shinnecock knowledge of waterfowl

The Shinnecock Elders’ resource catalogue lists black ducks among local waterfowl. Its broader waterfowl account describes decoys made from reeds and later carving in wood, naming Charles Sumner Bunn and Lyle G. Smith as Shinnecock carvers.3

A black duck becomes a decoy

Shelburne Museum’s exhibition identifies a black duck decoy by Charles Sumner Bunn bearing Newbold Leroy Edgar’s brand. A bird’s recognizable form could become both a working tool and a record of a carver’s livelihood.4

Living Shinnecock artistry

Lyle G. Smith continues the carving tradition. Christian Weaver’s 2023 profile connects his work with his uncle Norman’s carving and the hunting guides in his family. Lyle and his mother, painter Gloria Smith, have exhibited together at Southampton Arts Center.5

Explore Duck Decoys for the longer history and dated Historic Moments, and Alice Bunn Martinez for the family memory behind Bunn’s work.

Look at shape and movement

Watch how a duck holds its head, floats, and lifts into flight. Which details would a carver need to notice? The map’s decoy-shaped silhouette offers a starting point; the wetlands and the art each tell more of the story.

The moving animal is an illustration of habitat and movement, not a live sighting or a route to wildlife.

Knowledge recorded by Shinnecock elders in 2014

Black ducks, mallards, and mergansers

The catalogue describes waterfowl returning to Shinnecock shorelines and a decoy tradition using reeds and, later, carved wood. It names Charles Sumner Bunn and Lyle G. Smith among Shinnecock carvers, connecting bird knowledge with artistic skill.6

Page references

The Shinnecock Environmental Department compiled this catalogue from elders’ memories and community resource knowledge in 2014. Food and medicine appear here as historical knowledge; safe identification and treatment require current guidance.

why_this_matters: Wetlands sustain birds and the cultural knowledge connected with them. Shinnecock decoy carving shows how close observation can become art, livelihood, and a legacy whose makers deserve recognition.
